newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanians scavenge through empty Rwandan camps.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanians scavenge through empty Rwandan camps.

text.p: Tanzanians scavenged through Rwandan refugee camps on Wednesday as refugees streamed back to Rwanda, bringing the total exodus to more than 235,000 in five days.
Hundreds of civilians emerged from Benaco, Lumasi and Lukole camps burdened with large amounts of booty pilfered in the wake of the refugees pushed home by Tanzanian troops and police.
Benaco, with a population of 160,000, was Tanzania's second largest city until refugees started heading home on Saturday.
"The Rwandans left so I harvested their crop for them," said one man carrying a plastic bin overflowing with ripe tomatoes.
More than 100 Tanzanian civilians were carrying furniture out of Lukole camp including a woman with a desk on her head.
Paul Stromberg, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), said 28,000 Rwandans crossed into Rwanda from Tanzania by Wednesday evening, bringing the total to more than 235,000.
"We're feeling happy about going home but we are all tired of walking," said Innocent Ruhangara, 31, on the road with his wife and young son. "There's no way out except back to Rwanda."

Like most other refugees he said he hoped to find the home they fled in 1994 still empty. But many returnees among the more than 800,000 to return from Tanzania and Zaire in the last five weeks are finding their houses occupied by other Hutus.
On the main road to the Rusumo border crossing into Rwanda, UNHCR workers threw high protein biscuits to the returnees.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies however said about 100 children every day were losing their parents in the crush of refugees heading for the border.
UNHCR said on Wednesday it was suspending indefinitely night operations after a Rwandan soldier fired on a U.N. convoy.

U.N. officials said no one was hurt in the incident, which occurred on Tuesday night at a Rwandan checkpoint 19 km (11 miles) inside Rwanda from Tanzania, and said they did not expect the suspension to reduce the numbers trucked to their homes.

Officials said a truck stopped at a Rwandan checkpoint but its driver did not set the hand-brake so it rolled into a pickup in the U.N. convoy, prompting a soldier to fire. The convoy was returning to the border after dropping off refugees.
"It was an unfortunate incident," said Stromberg, adding UNHCR officials were raising it with the Rwandan authorities.
Aid officials said a large group of refugees was emerging from the bush about 90 km (55 miles) southeast of Ngara and starting the march north towards the Rusumo crossing point.
"These people are ill, cold and hungry -- that's why they are coming out," said UNHCR spokeswoman Judith Melby, adding refugees in the Karagwe region to the north were also heading for the border.
Most of the 125,000 refugees in the Karagwe region will have to walk about 250 km (150 miles) to the Rusumo border crossing.

Former Rwandan Hutu Interahamwe militiamen and troops refuse the Tanzanian deadline of December 31 for all 540,000 Rwandan refugees to return to Rwanda, saying they will be attacked or jailed for their part in genocide of minority Tutsis in 1994.
The exodus from Tanzania follows the return of an estimated 600,000 Hutu refugees from eastern Zaire, where a Tutsi-led rebellion forced them to abandon their camps last month.

The refugees left Rwanda in 1994 when troops, militiamen and mobs slaughtered some 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Rwandan Tutsi rebels then drove them out of the country and formed the present government.
